The second process is completely different.

Here too, the philosopher himself need not take an active part. He may simply observe the process passively and describe it. But in observing it he discovers that the process would not exist at all without human action.
If nature alone “acted,” then flying across the ocean would have remained a false human opinion—a fantasy. By nature, human beings have no wings and cannot fly.
This “natural” error could be turned into a truth only because human beings built an airplane—something that would never have existed in nature without them.
In short, the temporal dialectical process capable of turning a false human opinion into genuine knowledge is nothing other than the process of human work.

Clearly, if we applied to this second dialectical process the same principle that Greek philosophy and natural science apply to the first, absolutely nothing would remain of the human and historical world.

If we removed everything that human work has created over the course of time, what would remain would be only the animal body in which the first human being somehow, somewhere, and at some point “came into being.”

What distinguishes human beings from that animal today is precisely the conditions of life they have created over time. Human life differs from animal life because human beings have transformed the conditions under which they live.

So to eliminate from knowledge everything that changes with time would amount to eliminating everything that concerns the human being as human, together with the specifically human—that is, social and historical—world.
What would remain would be knowledge of nature alone, and even that would be only a schematic and simplified knowledge of nature.

Since philosophy studies not only the natural world but also the human world, it must therefore take account of both dialectical processes. And it cannot simply discard everything that changes in accordance with either process.

Philosophy knows, of course, that the natural world, through its spatial existence and temporal development, can confirm or refute human judgements about nature. Until nature itself has provided this confirmation or refutation—which, as we already know, can be obtained only through experiment and technology—philosophy must treat human judgements as mere opinions.
But philosophy also knows that nature ceased to be wholly unchanged from the moment human beings appeared on Earth.

Through work, humanity changes the face of the natural world and creates within it a historical world of its own. This historical world is no less real than the natural world, although its existence depends on human knowledge, human will, and human activity.

Human beings do not merely adjust their knowledge to the world through a cognitive and contemplative process. Through a creative and active process, they also change the world in order to bring it into line with their knowledge.

The philosopher must take this into account. He cannot regard everything that fails to correspond to the given form of the natural world as a final error, because he knows that human beings may transform that world through work.
He must understand that human opinions are not merely “hypotheses” about what already exists. They are also projects indicating what ought to exist in the future.
And he must therefore recognize that opinions become knowledge not only through comparison with nature but also through the creation of the human world.

In any case, once philosophy includes within its knowledge the human being and the historical world human beings create, it can no longer consign everything that changes over time to the realm of “personal opinions.”
If philosophy seeks to know the human world, it must also take account of the fact that although the world is one way today, it may be different tomorrow.
The whole problem, then, is this:
How can we distinguish such knowledge—whether true or false—from mere opinion?
We already know how matters stand with knowledge of nature.

The philosopher must regard as an opinion or a problem anything that has not undergone active experimental and technical verification. Whatever can be successfully incorporated into the natural world through such verification must be regarded as true knowledge. Whatever nature itself, so to speak, rejects must be treated as false.

Of course, it will be possible to divide all possible opinions about nature once and for all into true and false only at something like the “end of time,” when human beings have actually realized everything they are capable of realizing—that is, everything internally consistent and compatible with what already exists in the world.
Before then, however, it is still possible to establish that some opinions about nature constitute true or false knowledge.
Things are quite different when it comes to knowledge of the human world.
Because here there is no unchanging framework that would allow us to establish even partial but final knowledge of the kind we can establish about nature.
We have already discussed this problem when we said that the technical verification of knowledge about nature corresponds to the political verification of knowledge about the human world.
We saw that political verification cannot be regarded as final, precisely because the state itself changes over time, whereas nature remains unchanged—at least in its fundamental laws.
It may therefore seem that in the field of knowledge about the human world, only opinions are possible.
A simple example will make the point clear.
Imagine that under some existing state, an ordinary man assassinates its ruler. After committing this terrible crime, he is tried and condemned as a criminal.

Suppose, however, that this murder becomes the catalyst for a revolution that overthrows the regime represented by that state. The murderer now becomes a hero and is rewarded as such by the new government.
What, then, is this man “in reality”: a murderer or a hero?
And what does it mean to regard him, say, as a criminal? Is that judgement merely an opinion? Is it a truth? Or is it an error?
Knowing everything about the man’s actual deed clearly does not answer the question. Nor can political verification settle it once and for all.
The revolutionary government might itself be overthrown, in which case the murderer, having become a hero, could become a criminal once again.
Since every state can in principle change its regime, no state can ever settle this problem definitively.
Suppose that today, during a solar eclipse, someone runs through the streets of Moscow shouting loudly, waving his arms strangely, and furiously beating a musical instrument.
“What on earth are you doing?” people ask.
“I’m trying to drive away the dragon that is eating the sun!”
He will be declared insane and treated accordingly. And there can be no doubt that this judgement about him will be true.
Yet if someone had behaved in exactly the same way five thousand years ago—or if he were not a Muscovite but a Papuan—then calling him insane would unquestionably be an error.
And why go so far away?

Is it not “natural” to regard as disturbed someone who claims that the perfectly good bread baked today in a Moscow oven is actually a piece of the corpse of a Jew who died in Palestine roughly two thousand years ago?
And yet we still cannot simply make that judgement about the Christian. Although we know that he is mistaken, we cannot treat him in the same way as an ordinary psychiatric patient.
The first shows that we may know everything about a person’s actual deed without being able to determine whether he is a criminal or a hero.
More precisely, any judgement on the question will remain a personal opinion and therefore completely open.

To pass from subjective opinion to objective knowledge, we must place the man and his deed within the society and state to which he belongs and ask what that society and state think of him and of what he did.
In other words, I will regard the deed as heroic or criminal according to how the society in which it was committed evaluates it.
By doing this, I unquestionably move beyond the limits of personal opinion.
If that society were as eternal and unchanging as the natural world, I would thereby arrive at knowledge.

But society changes. Indeed, it may change partly because of the way it evaluates this very murder. So in appealing to society, I do not reach knowledge. I merely replace my own personal opinion with society’s opinion.
And it seems that I can go no further.
At first glance, the second example produces a similar result. I may know perfectly well how a person behaves and what he claims, yet still be unable to determine whether or not he is insane.
To move beyond my personal opinion, I must once again place his claims within the society to which he belongs and judge him “mad” or “normal” according to the judgement of that society.
Here too, I can replace my personal opinion with society’s opinion, but I appear to have no way of reaching final and necessary knowledge.
If someone’s assertions concern nature, experimental and technical verification can in principle establish whether they are true or false.
We therefore know that the claims in our examples concerning the solar eclipse and transubstantiation do not correspond to reality and are false.
But this verification gives us knowledge of nature—of the sun and of bread—not knowledge of the people around us.
We know that these people are mistaken, but we cannot thereby know whether they are “normal.”

Yet knowing whether someone is mentally ill or sane, whether he is a criminal or a hero, is at least as important and interesting as knowing the mechanism of a solar eclipse or the chemical composition of bread baked today.

And if the claims themselves concern the human world, then we are unable either to determine once and for all whether those claims are “normal” or even to judge definitively whether they are true or false.
Plato, for example, demanded that private property be abolished in the ideal state and that wives and children be held in common.
In his own time, and for a long period afterward, this was regarded—if not as outright insanity—then at least as impossible or “utopian,” and therefore socially, politically, and historically false.
Today, however, any citizen of the Soviet Union will say that Plato’s first demand is unconditionally true and his second unconditionally false.

But insofar as such a citizen cannot explain why this is so—and we must admit that most could not—then we have to recognize that he speaks this way simply because this is the judgement of the society around him.
If we suppose that the society to which he belongs is not final, we must therefore say that we still do not know whether Plato was right.
And if we suppose that changes in the social and political order continue “forever,” then we must say that we will never know.
The general conclusion can be stated as follows.
A person who makes genuinely and radically new claims—claims that contradict the basic principles his society regards as true—must be judged insane by that society.
And if the same person performs an actual deed that threatens the existence of the society in which he lives, that society must treat him as a criminal.

The philosopher, however, knowing that historical dialectic exists, will for the time being treat the judgements of that society as mere opinions—opinions that may one day, though not immediately, turn out to be either true or false knowledge.
The historical dialectic through which the philosopher “calls into question” what a society regards as final knowledge works as follows.
We have already seen that through work, by changing the real natural world, human beings can turn something that was originally an error into a truth.
It is now easy to see that through struggle, in the broad sense of the word, by changing the form of the social and historical world, they can achieve a similar result.

Suppose someone struggles to impose his own views, even views initially regarded as insane. If he eventually wins—if one day he succeeds in convincing the surrounding society that he was right—then society will cease to regard him as mentally disturbed because of those views.

The philosopher will then be able to say that “in reality” this person was not mad at all but a great innovator—a “genius.” To have called him insane was therefore not merely an opinion rather than knowledge; it was a false opinion.
Conversely, if the person never manages to convince anyone that he is right, the judgement that he was insane will appear to be confirmed.
The same applies to the criminal.

If, after committing his crime, he struggles against society and wins that struggle—if he succeeds in changing society so that it comes to regard his deed not as criminal but as heroic—then he is no longer a murderer but a great revolutionary.
Conversely, if the society with which he comes into conflict does not change as a result of his actions, it will be possible to regard him “in reality” as a criminal.
All this would work perfectly if there had been only one revolution in the world—whether intellectual or political.
But since there have been many revolutions, and since we do not know how many more there will be, we cannot regard any of these dialectical solutions as final knowledge.
Using this dialectical method, we can in practice distinguish madmen and criminals with little risk of error.
But in principle we cannot be certain that we possess genuine knowledge.
